newsitem.title: KENYA: UK firm wins tender to supply Kenya 80,000T maize. [CORRECTED 15:08 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UK firm wins tender to supply Kenya 80,000T maize. [CORRECTED 15:08 GMT]

text.p: International Commodity Dealers (1993) Ltd (corrects name of company) has won a tender to supply Kenya with 80,000 tonnes of maize, the state National Cereals and Produce Board said on Wednesday.
The first consignment of 25,000 tonnes would arrive at the port of Mombasa around Tuesday next week and was sourced from South Africa, the board said in a statement read to Reuters.
"International Commodity Dealers won the tender because of the price they quoted and their past record in fulfilling contractual agreements with the board," it said.
"(They) beat four other companies that bid," said the board without giving more details.
International Commodity Dealers quoted a price of $180 per tonne, the board said. It added that the first consignment of 25,000 tonnes would arrive in Mombasa aboard the MV Melodia.
"More of the balance of maize imports will also be sourced from South Africa or the southern Africa region," the board said.
The Board had tendered for the purchase of maize on April 22. It said delays in announcing the winner and subsequent shipments were caused by logistics and legal reasons.

Prolonged drought in eastern and northeastern provinces of Kenya and a huge production deficit prompted President Daniel arap Moi to declare a national dissater and invoke emergency laws in some areas in January.

Seasonal long rains which started in March have not been sufficient and there are fears in the agricultural sector of serious food shortages for most of this year and early parts of next year, according to agriculture ministry officials.

Government food handouts to populations in Northeastern and Eastern provinces as well as the Rift Valley, Nyanza and Western continue. The government has removed duty from commercial maize imports to stimulate private sector participation in imports.

The Famine Early Warning System (FEWS), a project of U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), said in a report for June that a unusual lack of rainfall after the first week of Nay was causing considerable concern, especially in the high potential major maize producing districts in western kenya.
"The principal maize crop is showing signs of moisture stress," FEWS said.

"The absence of rainfall during its critical floowering stage has resulted in the falling off of flowers especially in the lower drier areas," FEWS said. "Further, the delayed application of calcium ammonium nitrate fertiliser was expected to lower the yields of the early planted crop."
The board said some of the maize deficit was being adequately covered by private sector imports.

But FEWS said: "despite large commercial imports, the upward pressure on the price of maize has persisted in most of the country -- most of the imported maize has been purchased by millers. High prices are expected to persist until September."
FEWS quoted maize prices at around 1,600 Kenyan shillings ($29.35) per 90 kg (198.45 lb) bag compared to 600 shillings per bag in May 1996.
